transcription:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-05-28 15:00 PT
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Anita, Tom, Javier (Blueforge)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference. Quick sound check?
[00:07] Anita: Hi Maya, audio's good. This is Anita, we run the ML team at Blueforge.
[00:10] Tom: Tom here, backend.
[00:12] Javier: Javier, product.
[00:13] Samir: Samir on the call, I'll do most of the demo and deep dive on streaming and retries.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. Goal today is a short walkthrough of hosted chat streaming basics, tuning params, and a retry playbook so your infra folks can feel confident. We'll leave time for Qs.
[00:33] Javier: We're mostly concerned with triage assistant — it's low latency, like under 200ms p50 for short prompts, and we care about cost. Also data residency questions.
[00:43] Samir: Great, that's helpful. I'll start with the request/response shape for streaming. We typically recommend streaming via Server-Sent Events or websockets, depending on your client. With SSE you get incremental tokens as they arrive.
[00:55] Tom: Quick question — does Redwood support chunk reassembly if a stream drops mid-response?
[01:00] Samir: Good question. On the hosted API we provide a reconnect token. If you reconnect within a short window the server can resume from the last acknowledged token using the KV cache. Sometimes transcripts show K-V cash in the auto transcript, but it's KV cache.
[01:14] Anita: So if a mobile client loses network for 2–3s it can pick up?
[01:17] Samir: Exactly, that's the pattern. But we also recommend idempotency keys on the request so if you retry from client you don't double-charge or duplicate completions.
[01:25] Maya: Also worth noting, console shows the per-request token breakdown so you can quickly see tokens used vs cached usage, which helps cost tuning.
[01:34] Javier: Can you demo the console traces?
[01:36] Samir: Yep. Pulling up the console now — excuse the screen share bandwidth. (screen noise)
[01:45] Samir: Alright you can see the request timeline: recv time, model selection, kernel warmup, and token stream. The trace shows when we hit a cached prefix so the effective token compute drops.
[01:57] Tom: That's useful — and latency queues?
[01:58] Samir: We surface queue times and batching windows. If you set aggressive batching you can get better amortized cost but you incur a bit more p95 latency. For your triage case we recommended minimal batching at first and maybe prefix caching.
[02:10] Anita: What about params —temperature/top_p/max tokens — any defaults we should start with?
[02:15] Samir: For deterministic triage we suggest temperature 0.0–0.2, top_p ~0.8, max_tokens tuned to your prompt size. Start with 0.0 if you need repeatability. Also stop sequences for structured outputs.
[02:29] Javier: Do you have patterns for short-response optimization?
[02:32] Samir: Yes, few tips: send concise system+user messages, use shorter max_tokens, use streaming with early stop when end-of-sentence token seen, and use prefix KV cache. That typically reduces tokens by 20–40% depending on repetitiveness.
[02:47] Maya: I'll note that caching gains depend on how repetitive your prompts are. If every prompt is unique you won't see the same drop.
[02:56] Tom: How do we handle retries on 5xx or rate limits?
[02:59] Samir: Our recommended playbook: on 429 or transient 5xx, exponential backoff with jitter, and use idempotency tokens for safe retries. For streaming, try a resumable reconnect first, then fall back to a full request with the same idempotency token.
[03:14] Anita: Any hard recommendations for initial backoff params?
[03:17] Samir: Start with base 200ms, factor 2 exponential, max cap ~5s with full jitter. So 200ms, 400ms, 800ms... randomize each interval. That handles thundering herd.
[03:28] Javier: How about cost monitoring? We mentioned token-level cost in the console, can we alert on regression?
[03:35] Maya: Yes, Optimize console has quality and cost monitors — you can tie regressions to prompt sets and get alerts for token usage spikes. We can enable that in the pilot.
[03:43] Tom: Security: how is data retained on hosted? We need SOC2 and log redaction.
[03:49] Maya: We are SOC 2 compliant. Hosted API can be configured with short retention and optional request-level redaction. For highly regulated flows we recommend Redwood Dedicated or Private deployment. We'll share the security pack.
[04:03] Anita: We'll want detail on encryption/KMS too.
[04:06] Maya: Noted, will include KMS integration notes.
[04:09] Samir: Back to streaming specifics — one subtlety: if you have a long context that requires KV cache, we do chunking of the KV cache for performance; some clients mis-handle chunked state on reconnect, so test reconnect flows in the sandbox.
[04:23] Tom: What about tokenization differences across models? We use a lot of medical shorthand.
[04:27] Samir: Tokenization differs by model, and that affects max tokens and pricing. We'll show tokenization in the console so you can see char->tokens for samples. For medical shorthand, we suggest a small eval set to measure hallucination risk when you do quantization.
[04:42] Javier: Speaking of quantization — can hosted models be quantized?
[04:45] Samir: Hosted catalog includes some quantized variants with Redwood-verified perf profiles. For critical accuracy we usually recommend full precision or lightly quantized. Optimize can recommend quantization profiles based on your eval workload.
[04:58] Anita: Could you run through a broken-stream example? We want to see both resume and full-retry.
[05:02] Samir: Sure. I'll trigger a simulated network drop from the client side and then show reconnect in the trace.
[05:08] [screen noise / demo actions]
[05:12] Samir: Ok I dropped the stream; console shows a partial response with last ack at token 43. Client reconnect tries resume token and we replay tokens 44+. In parallel, the server marks the earlier stream as closed so there's no double billing.
[05:26] Tom: Nice. If resume window is missed, then what?
[05:30] Samir: If outside resume window the client should do a full retry with same idempotency key; server dedupes by idempotency and returns the already-completed output or re-runs if allowed by your policy.
[05:42] Maya: We sometimes recommend clients persist a small local buffer of completed chunks to present instantly on reconnect while background reconciliation happens.
[05:51] Javier: What are common mistakes you've seen in implementations?
[05:55] Samir: Three big ones: 1) No idempotency tokens so duplicate completions; 2) No jitter in backoff leading to synchronized retries; 3) assuming streaming always beats sync — sometimes synchronous short calls are simpler and lower cost for tiny prompts.
[06:11] Anita: For our triage assistant, most prompts are <100 tokens. Would you suggest streaming or sync?
[06:16] Samir: For sub-100 token short responses, sync with a small timeout might be fine — it eliminates stream resume complexity. But if you need partial progressive render for the UI, stream. The latency tradeoffs are small either way.
[06:29] Javier: Let's talk about concurrency and rate limits — we have spikes during incidents.
[06:33] Maya: For spikes we recommend reserved bursts with Dedicated or burst capacity on hosted. Also rate-limit headers from the API help client throttle gracefully. We'll demo headers in the sandbox.
[06:45] Tom: How does dedicated vs hosted change the retry story?
[06:48] Samir: Dedicated reduces multi-tenant noise and you get more predictable queue times. Retries still apply for network and transient infra events but you'll see less 429s. For strict SLOs Dedicated or Private is recommended.
[06:59] Anita: On monitoring, can we export traces to our internal observability (e.g., Datadog)?
[07:03] Maya: Yes, console supports webhooks and trace export. We'll include the integration doc.
[07:09] Javier: Are there rate-limited endpoints for embedding vs chat?
[07:12] Samir: Different endpoints have different rate limits; split traffic model is common — route embeddings to embedding pool, chat to chat pool. Smart routing prevents noisy neighbors.
[07:22] Tom: Could you show param tuning in the request payload?
[07:25] Samir: Sure — here's a sample JSON: {model: "rwd-chat-medium", messages: [...], temperature:0.1, top_p:0.8, max_tokens:128, stream:true, idempotency_key:"bf-triage-20260528-01"}. Sometimes the transcript misreads the model as redward, but it's rwd-chat-medium.
[07:47] Anita: If we enable streaming with stop tokens, do you ever see partial outputs missing final punctuation?
[07:53] Samir: Occasionally yes — stop sequences can truncate abruptly. We recommend post-processing with a short recheck: if last token isn't punctuation, request a small follow-up with the same idempotency token to complete.
[08:05] Javier: Any suggestions for client SDKs?
[08:08] Samir: We have official SDKs in Python, Node, and a lightweight JS streaming helper. For mobile we suggest websocket wrappers that handle reconnect and idempotency.
[08:19] Tom: Do you provide sample code for exponential backoff and jitter?
[08:22] Samir: Yes, there's a retries snippet in the docs. I'll paste it in the follow-up.
[08:28] Maya: Quick pause for any security follow-ups. Anita?
[08:31] Anita: KMS integration detail please. Also audit logs — do you preserve full prompt text in logs?
[08:37] Maya: Audit logs store metadata by default; you can opt-in or opt-out to store full prompt text. For SOC 2 customers we recommend encrypted logs with KMS and shorter retention. We'll put the security pack in the next email.
[08:49] Javier: Great. Could we discuss a small pilot — wanted about 3 weeks, run 10k requests/day to validate latency and cost.
[08:58] Maya: That sounds doable. We'll give sandbox access and run the microbench. Samir will help set up the sample harness.
[09:05] Samir: I'll prepare a minimal harness that hits the streaming endpoint with configurable packet drops so you can validate resume behavior.
[09:12] Anita: Awesome. On SLA, what's the hosted SLO?
[09:15] Maya: Host SLO is 99.9% for the hosted API for connectivity; p50/p95 latencies vary by model but we'll include a model profile. For harder guarantees, Dedicated/Private has contract SLOs.
[09:29] Tom: One more — we use a mix of synchronous and async frontends. Any advice for mixing both?
[09:34] Samir: Keep idempotency keys consistent across both. For sync path use a timeout fallback to async queuing for very long calls. And treat streaming as progressive UX enhancement.
[09:46] Javier: Can console show per-route quotas?
[09:48] Maya: Yes, per-route quotas and usage dashboards. We can lock per-route concurrency too.
[09:54] Anita: Let's do a quick run-through of the sample payload and then wrap.
[09:58] Samir: OK I'll send the sample payload now on chat. (typing) Sample flow: system message sets assistant role, user message includes patient note, temperature 0, stream true, idempotency key, stop sequence '\n'
[10:15] Samir: I'm going to run a short live request so you can see streaming in the console.
[10:18] [demo: live request triggered]
[10:22] Samir: Response streaming in, tokens at 12, 36, 59... you see partial suggestions appear in product UI.
[10:31] Tom: latency looks good.
[10:33] Maya: Wrapping up, recap and next steps: Maya to send retry/playbook docs and security pack, Samir to run bench and provide harness, Anita to provide sample prompts.
[10:46] Javier: Sounds good. Thanks, this is super helpful.
[10:49] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot kickoff.
[10:54] Anita: Thanks everyone.
[10:56] [meeting end]
